teaser: One painter turned this job down in horror. The next one made it the emblem of an age.
review_notes:
The commission story (Doyen's refusal, the bishop, the patron's instructions) comes from Charles Collé's journal, October 1767. The patron is traditionally identified as the baron de Saint-Julien but this is not certain; the lesson leaves him unnamed.
The older man is often called the husband; the lesson says this is a reading, not a fact.
Lord Hertford bought the painting at the duc de Morny sale in Paris, 1865.
Disney's Frozen (2013) reference: Anna imitates the pose in front of a version of the painting during a song.
Yinka Shonibare, The Swing (after Fragonard), 2001, Tate.
Falconet's Menacing Love (1757) was made for Madame de Pompadour.

lesson.text: In 1767 a respected Paris painter named Gabriel-François Doyen was summoned by a gentleman of the court. Doyen painted saints and miracles for churches. The gentleman, sitting beside his mistress, explained what he wanted instead. Doyen was so shocked that he refused on the spot. He did have one suggestion: try Fragonard.

The order was precise. Paint Madame on a swing. Have a bishop push her. And place me, said the client, where I can see this lovely girl's legs, or more if you want to make the picture livelier. For a painter of altarpieces, it was an insult. For a certain kind of talent, it was a gift.

Jean-Honoré Fragonard was 35. Two years earlier he had triumphed with a huge, tragic scene from ancient history, the sort of picture that led to official glory. Then he drifted away from that path. State payments came late, and private collectors paid quickly for smaller, lighter, naughtier things. He said yes.

We know the story because a playwright, Charles Collé, met Doyen a few days later and wrote the conversation down in his journal. The client's name is still debated, which is probably how he would have wanted it.

Fragonard changed one thing. The bishop disappeared, replaced by an older man in plain clothes. Everything else in the order is there, and it is arranged with the care of a stage director. Three people, each given a corner and a part to play.
Trace how the three figures are tied together.

lines.label: A triangle
lines.text: The young man lower left, the woman at the top, the older man lower right. She is the peak, and the only one fully in the light.

lines.label: The pull
lines.text: From the shadows, the older man works two cords attached to the seat. He provides the motion. From where he sits, he cannot see who is hiding in the bushes.

lines.label: The reach
lines.text: The young man's arm shoots up, hat in hand, pointing exactly where the client asked to be allowed to look.

lines.label: The swing ropes
lines.text: The ropes slant instead of hanging straight down. She is at the top of her arc, the split second when a swing stops before falling back.

lesson.text: So the picture is a small machine. One man powers it without knowing what it does. The other man profits from it. The woman, at the top of the arc, looks down at her lover, not back at the one pulling. Whether he is her husband, as people often say, the painting does not tell us.
At the top of an arc, loose things keep going. Something has just left her and is still in the air.
An object is flying through the garden. Can you catch it?

spots.title: The slipper
spots.text: A tiny pink shoe, spinning against the green mist. She has kicked it off her left foot, which is still pointed, toe bare in its white stocking.

lesson.text: A lost shoe was an old, well-understood joke about lost restraint. And look at where it is heading: toward a statue on a pedestal at the left edge. That statue is a quotation. Parisians of 1767 would have recognized it.

The statue copies a real marble: “Menacing Love” by Étienne-Maurice Falconet, carved in 1757 for Madame de Pompadour, the king's mistress. It was one of the most reproduced sculptures in France, sold as small porcelain figures.
Fragonard filled the garden with stone and fur witnesses. Each reacts to the scene in its own way, like a chorus commenting on a play.

lesson.title: Who else is watching
lesson.text: Three bystanders, from left to right.

spots.title: Cupid says hush
spots.text: The winged god of love sits on his pedestal with a finger pressed to his lips. He has seen everything and asks us to keep the secret.

spots.title: Two stone children
spots.text: A pair of cherubs ride a dolphin. One stares up at the swing with a worried face. The other looks away.

spots.title: The little dog
spots.text: A white lapdog stands at the older man's feet, head up, barking at the swing. Dogs stood for faithfulness. This one raises the alarm and is ignored.

lesson.text: The garden itself joins in. Nothing is trimmed. Branches twist like arms, roses spill over, and blue-green mist fills the gap in the middle like stage smoke. This is the Rococo style at full strength, the 18th-century French taste for curves, pastel colors, pleasure and play.

The canvas is small, about 81 by 64 centimeters (32 by 25 inches). You could carry it under one arm. Against all that cool green, Fragonard sets a single warm shape: the dress. It is painted in quick, wet strokes of pink, cream and white, and it seems to give off its own light.

spots.title: The dress
spots.text: Layers of pink silk and white lace thrown open by the movement, like a flower in bloom. The frills are single flicks of a loaded brush.

spots.title: Her face
spots.text: Under a straw hat tipped by the wind, she looks down toward the roses with a small smile. She knows exactly who is there.

spots.title: The lover
spots.text: Flat on his back in the rose bush, in a gray silk suit with a pink flower in the buttonhole, cheeks flushed, mouth open.

spots.title: The older man
spots.text: Seated on a stone bench in the dark, smiling up at her, a cord in each hand. He thinks the game is his.

spots.title: The knot
spots.text: The ropes are tied around a thick, gnarled branch. Up close they are frayed and fuzzy, painted thread by thread.

spots.title: The light
spots.text: Sunlight breaks through a hole in the canopy at upper left and falls in a soft diagonal onto the swing, a spotlight for one actress.

spots.title: A rake
spots.text: Among the weeds at the bottom lies a gardener's rake, dropped and forgotten. Nobody has been tending this garden for a while.

lesson.text: The Swing tells its story the way theater does: through placement, light and props. Nothing improper is actually shown. The viewer puts it together, and becomes an accomplice.

The party did not last. After the French Revolution of 1789, this kind of painting stood for everything frivolous about the fallen aristocracy. Fragonard lost his clients and died in 1806, largely forgotten. In 1865 an English collector living in Paris, Lord Hertford, bought The Swing at auction. It has hung in London ever since.

The pose has had a long afterlife. In Disney's Frozen, Princess Anna leaps in front of a painting of it and copies the kick. In 2001 the artist Yinka Shonibare rebuilt the scene as a life-size headless mannequin in African-print fabric, shoe in midair.
As for Doyen, he went on painting large religious and historical scenes and kept his dignity intact. Today he is remembered above all for one thing: being the man who said no to The Swing.

quiz.question: Why did Fragonard get this commission?
options: Another painter, Doyen, refused it and suggested him
The king ordered him to paint it
quiz.explanation: Doyen, a painter of religious scenes, was shocked and passed the job on.

quiz.question: What did Fragonard change in the client's instructions?
options: He replaced the bishop with an older man in plain clothes
quiz.explanation: The bishop who was meant to push the swing disappeared.

quiz.question: What is the Cupid statue on the left doing?
options: Holding a finger to his lips
quiz.explanation: He asks for silence, as if keeping the lovers' secret.

quiz.question: What is flying through the air?
quiz.explanation: She has kicked off her shoe at the top of the swing's arc.

quiz.question: How do we know the story of the commission?
options: A playwright recorded Doyen's account in his journal
It is written on the back of the canvas
quiz.explanation: Charles Collé wrote down what Doyen told him a few days later.

quiz.question: What happened to Fragonard's reputation after the French Revolution?
options: He became court painter to Napoleon
He moved to London and grew rich
He lost his clients and died largely forgotten
quiz.explanation: His playful style came to stand for the fallen aristocracy.

facts.text: The Swing is a huge canvas, taller than a person.
facts.explanation: It is small, about 81 by 64 centimeters.

facts.text: The Cupid statue in the painting is based on a real sculpture by Falconet.
facts.explanation: It copies “Menacing Love,” carved in 1757 for Madame de Pompadour.

facts.text: The older man pushes the swing with his hands on the woman's back.
facts.explanation: He sits behind in the shadows and works it with two cords.
